heroHeadline: Trump-Xi Summit Closes Without H200 Deal or Signed AI Framework — SMIC Q1 $2.51B (+AI Shift), Hua Hong Commits $6B to Wuxi; MIIT Reaffirms Manufacturing-AI Integration; Post-Summit Chip Bifurcation Solidifies
heroSubtitle: The Trump-Xi Beijing summit (May 14–15, 2026) closed May 15 with warm rhetoric but no concrete technology outcomes — the single institutionalized output was the US-China AI safety dialogue channel announced May 14 by Treasury Secretary Bessent. Despite the US having approved approximately 10 Chinese firms (Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, JD.com, Lenovo) to purchase up to 75,000 Nvidia H200 chips each, zero chips have shipped. CNBC's post-summit Tech Download confirmed the chip issue is 'unresolved'; the proposed AI governance framework produced no signed document; and rare-earth exports from China remain approximately 50% below pre-restriction levels — Beijing continues wielding mineral flows as leverage. Time magazine called AI 'the elephant in the room,' noting that even with Jensen Huang personally recruited by Trump en route to Beijing via Alaska, no commercial breakthrough materialized. The H200 license reportedly requires Nvidia to remit 15–25% of China sales revenue to the US government — a commercial condition Beijing is using to justify directing Chinese firms toward domestic Huawei Ascend chips (which command ~60% of China's AI accelerator market and $12B projected 2026 revenue). Three China semiconductor earnings/strategy announcements on May 15 collectively define the post-summit reality: (1) SMIC Q1 2026 revenue $2.51B with Q2 guidance +14–16% QoQ driven by AI orders — smartphone share at its lowest since 2021, confirming the foundry's pivot to AI/industrial chips; (2) Hua Hong committed $6B to its Wuxi Fab 9B expansion despite the US April 29 order blocking 7nm tool shipments, pivoting to specialty analog/power/automotive chips where US chokepoints are weakest; (3) SCMP confirmed both major Chinese foundries are guiding Q2 growth led by AI demand — underscoring that domestic AI chip demand is driving capex independent of Nvidia access. On May 16, MIIT Minister Li Lecheng (Bloomberg) reaffirmed that China's manufacturing sectors must be modernized with AI and technology rather than eliminated — adding policy weight to Beijing's virtuous-circle strategy: AI-driven manufacturing demand → domestic chip demand → domestic fab investment → reduced strategic dependence on US hardware. The post-summit narrative is now clear: the US offered chip access China is refusing to take; China's foundry sector is accelerating regardless; and Beijing's industrial-AI integration deepens the demand-side case for the domestic chip ecosystem the summit failed to dislodge.
